concept.summary: Measure each tissue sample sequentially with an ATR probe (mid‑IR) followed immediately by a fluorimetric probe at the same spot; collect spectra, concatenate data, and build classification models (e.g., PCA, PLS‑DA).
concept.probe: ATR crystal probe for MIR, separate fluorimetric probe positioned at the same location
concept.location: Laboratory benchtop, sample placed on a flat holder; probe tip contacts tissue surface
concept.fiberLink: Standard silica fiber for MIR‑ATR (if needed) and multimode fiber for fluorescence
concept.analyzer: Mid‑IR FTIR spectrometer with ATR accessory and a fluorimeter module

citations.quote: The developed multispectral probe was tested in the practical analysis of biological tissue samples using diﬀerent organs and parts of the chicken: breast, fat, and liver.
The general chemical similarity of biological objects makes spectroscopic recognition of diﬀerent tissue types a nontrivial task, which requires careful optimization of the measurement technique.
Immersible fiber optic probes operating in various spectral regions from UV to mid-IR are increasingly being used for measuring liquid and soft or powdered solid samples.

citations.quote: r. The MIR-ATR component captures the "chemical fingerprint" of the tissue's surface layer, typically at a depth of few microns, providing information on molecular composition and biochemical changes.
The observed loss of intensity in the ﬂuorescence channel is due to a smaller number of detection ﬁbers, as dictated by the optimal geometry of the ATR crystal.

risks: Sequential measurements may still sample slightly different micro‑regions, affecting comparability.
ATR depth (~few µm) differs from fluorescence penetration depth, potentially leading to mismatched information.
Fluorescence signal may be weak for native tissue; may require excitation wavelength optimization.

steps: Prepare at least three replicates of each tissue type (muscle, fat, liver) as in prior studies【ref":"S04.3.8"】.
Acquire MIR‑ATR spectra on each sample using the ATR probe.
Immediately acquire fluorescence spectra at the same spot with the fluorimetric probe.
Preprocess (baseline correction, normalization) and concatenate spectra.
Build classification models (PCA, then supervised PLS‑DA) and evaluate performance on held‑out samples.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the concatenated data yield clearly separated tissue clusters (as shown in prior work【ref":"S04.4.3"】) and improve classification metrics over single‑method models, the combined approach is justified.
